articles.title: A Cleaner Test Case: Why Kahoot! Adds Fire to the Supreme Court’s Settled Expectations Docket
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The USPTO’s “settled expectations” policy now has a second challenger at the Supreme Court. On July 24, 2026, Kahoot! AS filed a petition for certiorari (docket number pending) asking the Court to review the Federal Circuit’s order in In re Kahoot! AS, No. 2026-119, 2026 WL 519635 (Fed. Cir. Feb. 25, 2026), a two-page per curiam mandamus denial from Judges Taranto, Mayer, and Stark. The petition presents the same two questions already pending in Google LLC v. VirtaMove, Corp., No. 25-1230:
Igor Timofeyev of Paul Hastings is counsel of record, joined by Naveen Modi and Rudy Kim. Ginger Anders of Munger Tolles filed the Google petition. Kahoot! asks the Court to grant and consolidate the two cases, or alternatively to hold its petition for Google. [Kahoot – Certiorari Petition with appendix.]
I wrote about the Google petition when it was filed and again when seven amicus briefs arrived in late May. The PTO waived its response, but the Court requested a response. The Solicitor General obtained an extension to August 12, 2026, while VirtaMove went ahead and filed its brief in opposition on July 13. A call for a response is no guarantee of anything, but it means at least someone at the Court wants the government to defend the policy before the petition is resolved. The two cases also offer a key factual difference with regard to settled expectations: Google’s challenged patents had been in force for more than fourteen years, while Kahoot!’s target was less than six years old on the day the IPR petition was filed.
Settled expectations entered PTAB practice through then-Acting Director Coke Morgan Stewart’s March 2025 interim workload memorandum, which listed “settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force” among the considerations for discretionary denial. The six-year benchmark emerged that June with an analogy to 35 U.S.C. § 286, which limits infringement damages to the six years before suit.
Congress used patent age exactly once in the IPR provisions, as a floor rather than a ceiling: a petitioner must wait for nine months after issuance to file, and after that the statute says nothing about a patent ever becoming too old to challenge. Kahoot! explains to the Court that an accused infringer often has no reason to study a patent, much less challenge it, until the complaint arrives, which is why the one-year litigation deadline of § 315(b) runs from service of the complaint.
All this is sitting within a larger structural shift: institution is no longer a Board decision. Petitioners argue that this has exacerbated the problem because institution now turns on one official’s discretion, exercised through unexplained notices and shielded from review by § 314(d).
The mandamus wall. The Federal Circuit’s February order broke no new ground. Relying on Mylan Laboratories Ltd. v. Janssen Pharmaceutica, N.V., 989 F.3d 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2021), and its precedential decision in Apple Inc. v. Squires, ___ F.4th ___, 2026 WL 406495 (Fed. Cir. Feb. 13, 2026), the panel held that § 314(d)’s “final and nonappealable” command leaves mandamus ordinarily unavailable absent a colorable constitutional claim, and that ultra vires arguments “cannot be a basis for granting the petition for mandamus.” The Kahoot! order was one of five mandamus denials the court issued in a single week in late February. See Dennis Crouch, Five Petitions, Five Denials: The Federal Circuit’s Mandamus Wall Grows Higher, Patently-O (Feb. 28, 2026).
What does a second petition add? Beyond a “me too,” Kahoot! offers the Court a cleaner and more aggressive application of the rule. In Google, a fourteen-year-old patent at least sits comfortably past any plausible line. Kahoot!’s patent was under six when the petition was filed; the agency reached six only by measuring age at the date of its own decision, a move the petition calls arbitrary twice over, both for the “arbitrary period of six years” itself and for measuring from the wrong date. If expectations can settle while a petition awaits a ruling, the six-year factor starts to look less like one flexible consideration and more like a statute of repose that the agency wrote for itself.
This is a situation where, I believe, the reviewability question is the stronger candidate for certiorari. The statutory authority question is interesting, but it only matters if some court can ever reach it. Under the Federal Circuit’s current framework, § 314(d) bars appeal and Mylan bars mandamus, which means the Cuozzo reservation for agency action exceeding statutory limits describes a form of review that no court can actually conduct.
The government’s response in Google is due August 12, and the Kahoot! petition should receive its docket number in the coming days. If the Court calls for a response here as well, both petitions will be ready for the Justices when they return for the long conference at the end of September.
= = =
The patent. The patent behind all of this is U.S. Patent No. 10,339,825, “System and Method for On-Line Academic Competition,” owned by Interstellar Inc., a small Chicago company that runs the AreteLabs quiz-competition platform. According to the complaint, founder Timothy Kelley conceived the idea in 2008 while volunteering as a rowing coach at his high school alma mater and set out to bring the trappings of scholastic sports (leagues, brackets, real time scoring) into classroom quizzing; the company’s flagship event, Math Madness, is patterned on the NCAA tournament, and the platform draws about 25,000 subscribers a year.
Representative claim 1 covers a system with a question database and a processor that assembles teams and leagues, delivers timed quiz questions, and displays a “real time scoreboard with time clock” tallying individual and team scores in live or asynchronous matches. The application was filed April 4, 2012, and the patent issued July 2, 2019, after seven years in prosecution.
The lawsuit. Interstellar sued both the Kahoot! Norwegian parent and its Austin-based U.S. subsidiary in June 2024. Interstellar Inc. v. Kahoot! EDU, Inc., No. 1:24-cv-00727-ADA (W.D. Tex.). The complaint asserts eight claims of the ‘825 patent against the Kahoot! platform – pointing to features added over the years such as team mode and podium scoring, and alleges willful infringement based on early 2024 correspondence in which Kelley raised the patent with a Kahoot! executive.
The stay fight. The district court stayed litigation awaiting the IPR outcome – and that issue has become a battleground for the parties. After the mandamus denial, Interstellar brought in new litigation counsel and moved for a scheduling order, which Judge Albright denied without prejudice in March while keeping the status-report obligations in place. Meanwhile, Kahoot! tried the other administrative track and requested ex parte reexamination of additional claims of the ‘825 patent – but the office denied that request.
Interstellar says Kahoot! has now lost the IPR, Director Review, mandamus, and the reexam, accuses it of “stalling,” and points out that the underlying Google v. VirtaMove litigation is proceeding unstayed in the Northern District of California; Kahoot! answers that its appellate rights are not exhausted and asks the court to hold the stay in place at least until its cert petition is resolved.
